title: Wall Street's AI Party Hit a Wall: The Dow Dropped 537 Points as Inflation Fears Returned
excerpt: Spiking oil prices, a hawkish bond market and Jerome Powell's last day as Fed chair combined to deliver the sharpest selloff in weeks — with direct implications for NRI portfolios heavy on US equities.
body:
For weeks, Wall Street had been running on a single narrative: artificial intelligence would lift all boats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had touched record highs, propelled by hyperscaler spending and the conviction that generative AI would unlock a new productivity supercycle. On Friday, the market remembered that other things also matter.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 537.35 points, or 1.06 per cent, to close at 49,531.70. The S&P 500 lost 91.62 points (1.22 per cent) to settle at 7,409.62. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 412.61 points (1.53 per cent) to 26,226.35. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, the benchmark for AI-linked chipmakers, was dragged lower as Nvidia, AMD and Intel all ended sharply down.

## The Triple Squeeze

Three forces converged. First, crude oil prices surged after combative remarks from US President Donald Trump and Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi raised doubts about whether the fragile truce between Washington and Tehran would hold. Any disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly a fifth of global oil passes — would send energy prices spiralling further. Brent crude has been flirting with $109 per barrel, a level that feeds directly into transport costs, manufacturing inputs and, ultimately, consumer prices.

Second, Treasury yields jumped. The yield on the 10-year note touched its highest level since May 2025, when markets were reeling from Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement. Rising yields make bonds more attractive relative to equities, pulling capital out of stocks. More importantly, they signal that the bond market believes inflation is not going away.

Third, the Trump-Xi summit concluded in Beijing with atmospherics but few tangible outcomes. Beijing offered no clear assistance toward resolving the US-Iran conflict, and no new trade concessions materialised. "It seemed like more of a reset in relations and less short-term, quantifiable results," said Matthew Keator, managing partner at the Keator Group.

## The Powell Farewell

Friday also marked Jerome Powell's final day as Federal Reserve chair, closing a tenure that navigated the pandemic, the fastest rate-hiking cycle in four decades, and the return of inflation as a persistent concern. His successor, Kevin Warsh, inherits a policy environment that has shifted dramatically from the rate-cutting expectations that dominated markets at the start of the year.

The odds of the Fed *hiking* interest rates by 25 basis points in December have climbed to nearly 40 per cent, up from 13.6 per cent just a week ago, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. That is a remarkable swing — and one that directly contradicts the rate-cut narrative that had powered equity markets higher.

"The weakness today is highlighting the concerns that the recent numbers aren't transient," Keator said. "It's hard to envision the new chair communicating anything other than a neutral policy stance at best until we see some consistent, meaningful change in the data."

## What NRIs Should Watch

For Indian Americans and NRIs with exposure to US markets — whether through direct brokerage accounts, 401(k) retirement plans, or mutual fund SIPs in US-focused feeder funds — Friday's selloff is a reminder that the AI trade is not a one-way bet.

The correlation between US tech stocks and Indian IT services stocks means the damage does not stay on one side of the Pacific. When Nvidia and AMD fall, sentiment in Infosys, TCS and HCL Tech follows. With the rupee already at ₹96 to the dollar, NRIs remitting money home face a cross-current: a weaker equity portfolio in dollar terms, but a stronger dollar when converting to rupees.

The more structural concern is inflation. If oil prices remain elevated due to the Iran conflict and the Fed is forced to hike rather than cut, the cost of capital rises for everyone — from Silicon Valley startups seeking funding to Indian exporters borrowing in dollars. The AI supercycle may still be real, but markets have been reminded that it does not unfold in a vacuum.

Kenny Polcari, chief market strategist at Slatestone Wealth, put it bluntly: "There's a realization that the market had gotten way ahead of itself. It wasn't paying enough attention to what the bond market and economic data is telling it. It was caught up in this momentum AI trade."

The party is not over. But someone just turned on the lights.
